teaser.text: PayPal is a payments company: it helps people and businesses move money, and it earns fees when it completes those movements. To understand its business, follow a dollar from a shopper or sender to PayPal, through the costs and risks, and onward to the merchant, recipient or lender.

stock.opening: PayPal's weighted scenario reaches $67.00 in October 2027; the bear case has 30% probability, the base case 50% and the bull case 20%. It hinges on turning payment volume into durable margin while containing credit losses.
stock.closing: The full memo also answers how PayPal's business works, who its rivals are, how management is executing, and what risks could change the story.

blocks.heading: Where could PayPal's shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: The weighted forecast reaches $67.00 in October 2027. That implies +19%. It reaches $105.20 in October 2029. That implies +89%. The bear case has 30% probability, the base case 50% and the bull case 20%.
PayPal’s weighted path is $67.00 in October 2027, or a 19% return including dividends. It reaches $83.74 in October 2028, a 50% return, and $105.20 in October 2029, an 89% return.

blocks.heading: What has to go right for PayPal's base case—and what could go wrong?

paragraphs.text: The bear case requires branded checkout to keep losing shopper choice, while Braintree volume grows without enough transaction margin. Higher funding costs, credit losses or transformation spending then prevent savings from reaching profit. The first price is $50.42 in October 2027. The last is $58.22 in October 2029. Its probability is 30% because checkout grew only 2%, transaction margin dollars grew 1% and operating margin contracted.

The bull case requires checkout repair, stronger Venmo paid use, better-priced Braintree volume and savings that exceed reinvestment. The first price is $82.79. The final price is $165.16. Its probability is 20% because all four improvements must arrive together, while current transaction-margin conversion remains weak.

blocks.heading: How much cash does PayPal really make?

paragraphs.text: In Q2 2026, operating cash flow was $1,983 million and FCF was $1,775 million. PayPal’s adjusted FCF was $1,832 million after excluding the timing difference between originating BNPL receivables held for sale and selling them. In the first half of 2026, loan sales produced $15.8 billion of cash. That cash is real, but it is not automatically recurring cash from payment processing.

dividend.meta_description: PayPal's dividend began at $0.14 a share in October 2025; its 1.0% yield is shown against a $56.70 share price.
dividend.opening: PayPal's regular quarterly dividend began at $0.14 a share in October 2025, and the forecast holds it at $0.56 per share in the first forecast year. PayPal's payouts exceeded free cash flow in two of the five years shown, so cash coverage has not been consistent.
dividend.closing: The full memo also explains PayPal's business, its rivals, its management and its risks.

blocks.heading: How much does PayPal pay per share over time?

paragraphs.text: Buybacks and dividends return cash in different ways. A buyback sends cash to shareholders and retires shares, which gives each remaining share a larger ownership claim. A dividend sends cash without reducing the number of shares. PayPal authorized another $15 billion of buybacks in February 2025, but an authorization is permission to spend up to a limit, not a promise to spend it. It began its first regular quarterly dividend in October 2025 at $0.14 a share.

Dividends remain $0.56 per share in the first forecast year because the current quarterly payment is $0.14. The base case rises to $0.60 and then $0.64 through small annual increases. The bear case holds at $0.56 because the dividend is new and transaction-margin growth is weak. The bull case reaches $0.72 as stronger cash generation supports larger distributions, although no growth target has been promised.

blocks.heading: Is PayPal's dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: PayPal’s payouts exceeded free cash flow in two of the five years shown. That can happen when the company uses other cash sources or reduces cash elsewhere, but it creates a trade-off: money returned to shareholders cannot also fund investment or reduce debt.

blocks.heading: What is PayPal's dividend yield today against its price?

paragraphs.text: Buyback yield is 12.5%, versus a 1.0% dividend yield. 2025 repurchases exceeded PayPal’s free cash flow, while stock-based pay was $1.04 per share.

At $56.70 a share on October 18, 2026, PayPal looks cheap only if its current earnings reflect durable payment economics. The price assumes earnings hold near current levels, but the better test is how much PayPal keeps from each payment.

earnings.title: PayPal earnings: guidance and results
earnings.meta_description: PayPal's next results are expected on October 27, 2026; guidance covers margin, cash flow, repurchases, and checkout growth.
earnings.opening: PayPal's next results are expected on October 27, 2026. Watch whether branded-checkout growth improves while investment affects margins.
earnings.closing: The full PayPal memo also answers questions about PayPal's business, rivals, management and risks.

paragraphs.text: Transaction margin shows the strength of the payments engine. It is the money left from payment activity after direct processing costs and credit losses, but before expenses such as marketing and administration. A shop that collects $100, spends $55 on delivery and processing, and has $45 left before rent has created something like transaction margin. PayPal expects $15.6 billion of transaction margin for the year, or $14.5 billion excluding interest on customer balances. Removing interest gives a clearer view of payment performance because that income depends on interest rates and customer account balances.

Management expects non-GAAP non-transaction operating expenses to grow 7.0% to 8.0%, with an effective tax rate of 18.0% to 20.0%. It also expects adjusted free cash flow of $6.0 billion, plans $6.0 billion of share repurchases and expects $1.0 billion of capital spending. The test is whether checkout improves enough to support these plans while investment runs ahead of savings.

blocks.heading: What are PayPal's last eight quarters showing?

paragraphs.text: Revenue rose year over year, while operating income fell. Operating margin contracted 171 basis points to 16.4%. Net income and diluted EPS also declined because transaction expenses and other operating costs grew faster than revenue.

blocks.heading: What should PayPal watchers watch next?

paragraphs.text: The first checkpoint is Q3 earnings on October 27. Investors will compare revenue and EPS with expectations, but the more important evidence will be branded-checkout growth, customer engagement and the effect of investment on margins. Management expects savings to become more material in the fourth quarter, so later reports must show whether costs fall without starving the business of investment.

The long-term test is simple: checkout growth, customer engagement, savings achieved and continued loan-sale funding must improve together. PayPal’s newer ideas may matter later, but the next chapter will be decided first by whether the company can repair its core business while paying for the repair.
